title: Mr. and Mrs. A.C. Synigal and B. Bozant Interview, 1962-05-17
interviewee: Mr. and Mrs. A.C. Synigal and B. Bozant

pages.label: 001_Mr. and Mrs. A.C. Synigal and B. Bozant Interview, 1962-05-17 Part 1

blocks.x: We're recording today, May the 17th, 1962 at 1938 Laperoo Street. Could we get your names down here? You want my name? Your full name. Mrs. Edna. Thank you.

pages.label: 002_Mr. and Mrs. A.C. Synigal and B. Bozant Interview, 1962-05-17 Part 2

blocks.x: Let's see, this is a second reel and we're interviewing Madame Senegal and Madame Bozon. Am I getting it right?
Right, right.

That's right. Mr. Senegal and Miss Sandra have just stepped out for a minute. Let's see, better put today's date on here so we don't get it mixed up. May the 17th, 1962. Yes. By the way, this is your home here, isn't it? This is my home. We're calling it.
And by the way, it's the headquarters for the pre-old fiesta. This is headquarters.
See, in the weekly, they give us a dress.

That's right, headquarters. And we have a meeting room in patio. Next time you come, I'll bring you in the patio, babe. You can take notes of the patio, how nice it is. And then the meeting room, that's where we meet. I'll just let a few come in. And we have board meetings, you know, here. But our meeting room is really nice out there. We'll enjoy it. Now we are, what do you want to talk about, the fiesta? If he asked you.

You know what, we forgot to ask where you were born. I was born here in New Orleans. And as I said before, we have such customs. The house that I was born in, my father was born in. And my grandmother saw to it that all her children's children were born there. So, we were all born at 1510 Coord Street. My father and sisters and brothers. My grandmother went there as a bride. So she had all her children there and the children's children. She didn't care after the children were born. She said, now fine, get homes for yourself. But I wanted them to be born.
I just wanted a custom.
It's a custom, that's what it is. When did the fiesta start having parades and start having the Idol Fiesta? What year was it the first year?
The very first year.
It started right away? The first year.

From four people. From four people, we had a parade the very first year. And we had our first Mademoiselle Fiesta, the first year. We didn't call them queens then. We called them Mademoiselle Fiesta. That was the young girls. You know, you called them Mademoiselles. And so my granddaughter, Sylvia Serena, the daughter of the king of this year. King Edwin Serena was king this year. His daughter was the first Mademoiselle Fiesta. And we had the first parade then with five carriages. Five wagons. I had three carriages and wagons. We had those fruit. Those fruit wagons that you see those men selling? Yes. Well, we rented those. We had three of those with the children. And, oh, I have a picture. I'll look for it and show you the children who paraded in those wagons. It was all decorated with palms. I put a sheet on the wagon to cover it up and stuck palms all around. It was just beautiful. And some of the big girls now. Cynthia, who is the first, who was the maid this year to the queen, she rode in the wagon in the first parade. And wasn't that something after how many years ago? Oh, about, well, that's about seven, nine, or nine because we're ten years now. She rode in that first wagon with the little children. It was beautiful. So as the years go by, we began to expand, you see. So as it went on, we couldn't get the wagons anymore. So we had to get the, and the carriages. It was hard to get the carriages. And so we had to add these floats that we had this year. That was little children's floats. But didn't they look well? Didn't they look beautiful? Oh, yes. Well, they decorated them. And we had one for our queen, one for our king, and… Our future queens. Our future queens. Our future queens. The little girls who will be our future queens. And, of course, our carriages that the members rode in. So it's beginning to get larger all the time. And we have, we always have a convertible for our past queens. Because we want to go from the old to the new. See, we begin from the old. And the convertible, of course, is the latest. So we let the past queens ride in the convertible. With their escorts.
Wouldn't you like to tell him something about the soiree dancons? Oh, that's something that he doesn't know.
Do you know about these soirees and dancons?
I know what the words mean, but I don't know about them. I know a little bit of French.

Well, I'm telling you, I think we were the first to have them. I wouldn't swear to it, but I think we were the first to have the soirees. Huh? That's right. And I know of the papers, because… And, of course… We were the first.

At our soiree dancons, we always have lines waiting for collars. Yes. That's right. Collars. Like the ladies used to say, callars. Collars. Collars. And they really… The lady that made them, made them well. Of course, she's dead now.

She died. But we really miss her, because I think people came from… And we had our first outside affair was a block festival held in the streets. The city blocked off the streets from Prairie to Johnson. And they put up some booths in the streets. And we decorated them. And each had the hot dog booths and the ice cream booths for the children and different. And they had the barbecue booths. And the collars. They had the old time furnace. You remember old time furnace with the charcoal?
I don't know about that.
You don't know about the old time furnace? I've only been here 13 years.
Oh.
Well, here we were. Old time furnace with the charcoal. And here, we had two ladies there, cooking collars. Now this is… you want to know how that's made of? Oh, I'd love to know.
I know it has rice, but that's all I know. It's rice.

Overnight. And has to… I don't know really how it's made, but the lady told me. It's made overnight and it has to rise. And the next day, then you add some more flour or something to it. And make a batter of it. And it drops it like you drop… not pancakes, but anyhow, it drops in hot, hot lord. And it makes a little round thing. And this is collars. And we couldn't sell enough of them. The people who was in collars… We want collars… call them all kinds of names. We want collars. We want everything. Oh, we couldn't sell enough of those collars. So finally, the lady died. So we haven't had any. We didn't have any, Nancy. No more collars. And she… we asked her to give us the recipe. She promised and promised and didn't give us the recipe.
I think I might can find you the recipe. You think so?
We certainly would be glad.
I can find you. I think there's one… If you phone me at school, you still have my number at school?
I don't know.
But I'll write it down. Write it. Well, I'll write. And I think I have a recipe in a book. Is that so?
We certainly would like to get it.
There's a wonderful book called Gumbo Ya Ya, which describes all the customs… All those customs.

Well, we certainly would like to get that. Well, and they'd dance in the street. And then the Holy Family Sisters would come with their children and have the square dance. The sisters would come themselves and sit out on the porch here and they'll bring a band, a record. I think it was a record. And they'd get out in the street and they're right there in front of the door there. This is the headquarters for the fiesta. And they'd get out and dance, the square dance, at these block festivals. Now, that went on for several years until we got rained out. It rained for two years and we couldn't do anything. So, we decided not to be in the street anymore. So, after the block festival, then we went on to have the soiree dancin. That's right. And that was in the hall. In Autopilot. Autopilot hall. And that was nice. That was nice to have. It was French. And the people enjoyed that so much. So much. And after that, we had that at the Autopilot club. The soiree dancin. They were at the Autopilot club. Then we went on to the Wonderful Boys, let's name their homes.
We did because we couldn't get the Autopilot for that night. There was a mix up in the dates.
So, we went to the Wonderful Boys home. But you are not mirror, ma'am. Not mirror.

But usually, the soiree is just like we said before with the quadrille. You know, it's some parts that you really let your hand out. But the soiree dancin, we call it, that's our good time night. But of course, in a wonderful way. Because people come out to watch. I mean, it's a lot of fun. It really is. But in a nice way, of course. And then we have the tea.

Yeah. We begin our fiesta with a tea in September. We begin in September. Around the third Sunday, September? The third Sunday. In September. And it's always at the Autopilot club. They give us that date. The club, members of the club, give us the hall for that date. And, oh, we have a lovely tea. Tables are decorated, you know. And the board members are all in their regalia. Their big hats, flowers, and they serve at the tea tables. And we have, last year, we really almost had a concert. We had such nice singers. We had Oceola Blanchett. Do you know of him? He's a pianist. Professor Blanchett. Professor?
I know he used to play with Perez, Manuel Perez, years ago.
Professor Blanchett lives right at the next corner here.
Oh, I've always wanted to meet him. I never have met him. Oh, my.

Right on the next corner here. Very nice. He's on Sager and Ed Johnson. The next corner. And he plays for Deborah. And, well, he played for it. He went to school with my husband, huh? Oceola went to school with you. And so we mentioned about him playing for the tea. And some of the members says, Oceola Blanchett. I say, sure, why? He says, oh, he's a professor. He wouldn't give no time for a tea. You know, he's always so busy. I says, I'll bet you I can get him. So then I told my husband, he says, let them talk. He says, I went to school with Oceola, so I know I can get him. And he went there and he said, well, I was wondering why you hadn't asked me all these many years. He said, well, I know you're so busy all the time. I didn't want to worry. Well, you call me any time. And we had two girls who sang. Oh, that voice was beautiful. And the girl who was Queen, Mara Rego, she danced. She's a dancing teacher. You haven't met her, huh? Right here. She lives right in the next block. Oh, we have a lot of celebrities around here. Deborah Brown is just two blocks away on Turn T. And so I asked her. She came and danced for us. And we really had a lot. Oh, and the Woods Boys that sang on Ted Mack's show. The Woods Brothers. Yeah. Woods Brothers. And the Daddy. And the Boys. So, I know them since they were children. So I called them and, oh, Miss Senegal, we are honored to be asked by you to be in the Fiesta. So they came and they sang. And what other number we had? There was another number.
No, there are two good singers. We had one singer. Martha Saison. Martha Saison, that's right.

And Adrienne. Adrienne Rudolph. Rudolph. But Martha Saison is the star at Xavier Nair. She plays in all the concerts. Yeah. And so her father is a member with my husband of his lodge. And so he was so glad to ask his daughter. So we had a big concert instead of a tea. Everybody was sitting down. They were very much enjoyed by the tea we had.
I'd like to ask you about that very first year. What kind of music did you have when you said it was in Congo Square with some people called Borrigan?

What kind of music we had? We had Papa Salastare himself with Lizzie Miles singing. We had the best. The people start from the bottom up, but we had the best first. We had the best first. We've never had a concert like that since. But he donated his time. Well, I tell you how we got this Beauregard Square. Congo Square. I will call it Congo Square because I knew it by Congo Square. The Pops concert was going on. You know about the Pops concert. And so I went to see the mayor to ask for this square. And he was very busy at the time. And he told me to call up the scero, his assistant. Say, make an appointment with him. And he's very nice. He'll do just as I do. So I phoned him and made an appointment. And so when I got there, I said, what can I do for you, Mrs. Senegal? I said, oh, the sky's the limit. He said, I said, the sky's the limit. He said, well, that's all right. That's all right. We'll bring it down. I said, you just don't know what I came to ask you for. So he said, well, have a seat. Let's go. He said, well, go on, shoot. So I said, well, I came to ask you for Congo Square. He says, Congo Square? Where? What is Congo Square? I say, Congo Square? You don't know what is Congo Square? He says, no. He says, Washington Square, Lafayette Square, all the squares. He was named. I said, no, no. Well, where is Congo Square? I say, you're Lafayette Square, right in front of your municipal auditorium. A very large square. A very large square. A very large square. Right opposite your auditorium. He says, no, really? I says, yes, it is. I said, that's Congo Square. So he says, well, I never knew that before. I says, well, how do you know? He asked me how did I know that. I say, I was told that from my grandparents. And I know it's so because I have some people living today who told me that's where Marie Laveau used to do her dances on Sunday afternoon. And he says, that time, that time. I said, yes, I know what I'm talking about. It's not in the books. And I say, I know so well it's not in the books. Because I'm telling you something that it's not in the books that I know. So he says, well, if you know that much about Congo Square, what else you want? What else you got to tell me that I don't know of? I was, so he said, I said, well, now you have your pop concert going on now. Well, I'd like to have Congo Square Vow concert for the Fiestas, Creole Fiestas concert. He says, when? I says, well, we haven't set an exact date yet. He says, wait, let me tell. Well, I can help you. Wait a minute. He says, well, you know the pop concert is going on now. I said, yes. He says, well, if you can get your concert to come on immediately after the pops finishes, I will ask the head ones to leave all the lights, all the equipment, just as is for you to have your one night after. So I said, oh, that's fine. He said, but you have to go in. I'll ring them up. But you'll have to go yourself. I said, I'll go anywhere. Just send me. Just send me. So he sent me to the club on Rampart Street. The Y, Y MC on Rampart Street. Sent me there to Mr. Poche. I remember. That's his name. He told me to go see him because he was the chairman of that pop concert at that time. And asked him would he and his company or his associate would let me have the club on the day after they finished. So he told me he would call his men together. And lo and behold, he called me and said, yes, we could have it with everything as it stood. Everything. The loudspeaker and everything just as it stood. And no charges. With all the fence up and all the stage, the piano, everything just as it was. As long as we use it that night, we have to make our date the night after so it wouldn't stay so long. And he said, of course, they have to pay the man who will take care of it. You know, the, what do you call it? Night watchman. He said, now we can only pay one night for it. That's the night we are closing. So if you don't come on the night afterwards, they will close you down because we cannot pay for that night watchman. I said, we'll be there. Don't worry. We'll be there. So now, then I, I, we got it together and had our tickets and everything and we went on that night. Now we didn't, we didn't dance that quadrille that first night. We danced it the second year. The first year we didn't dance it for the first year. We had Papa Celisna. Well, I called him and I asked him, I said, what can you do for his Papa Celisna? He says, well, I'm telling you, if the city is so good to you and going to give you all that, I'm giving you my, my band for nothing. Now I'm coming out there with my band. And I phoned Lizzie Miles and she said, oh, well, you know, I should say this now. Papa Celisna said, she don't fool somebody else. She said, but I'll be there. I'll be there. I don't know. He didn't play much for her. I don't think something like that. But she says, I'll be there. And do you know they made friends that night? Papa Celisna said, Lizzie Miles made friends that night because she was playing for, Al Marico was playing for her, you know? Yeah. And so, well, he told me why. She didn't think he could play for her as some kind of, I said, well, as long as you admire, I don't care what you all do between you, but just be there and play for us, for our fiestas. So they did. And Papa Celisna began playing, what's her famous song? Billy? Bill Bailey. Bill Bailey.
Bill Bailey, once the piece come over.

They forgot whatever they had. Whatever they had, they forgot. Here was Lizzie Miles, Bill Bailey, and Papa Celisna, he said, now you know Miss Senegal, took you to bring us back together again. And they really, really did put it on that night. We really had a wonderful concert. That was the beginning of our fiesta, right there. And it was all given to us. Given to us. All given to us. From the city on down. And Mayor Maestrie, he sent word and he told me, anything we needed, we could have. Any city equipment that we needed, we could have. And so far, we've been having it. And we had a concert, as you spoke of, on Columbus Street.
At Claiborne? Claiborne and Columbus.
Claiborne and Columbus, yeah.
What year was that? Couldn't have been your second year. Oh, it was about the third.
Third year. It was about the third year. It was about the third year. It was the third year. Now, who played? He played then too? He's been playing all along. It was Papa Celisna's band.
He was all along. I don't remember if he was there.
He was there?
I don't know if he was there, but I remember his band.

They've been playing for us all along. You see, we had him this year for our dance. Albert French. Yeah, he's dead. Albert French has his band. I thought it was Eddie Pearson. It was Eddie Pearson. He died. So, it's Albert French then.
Is there any year you didn't use this band? No.

Used them every year since the fiesta began. But of course, as they died out, they replaced them. You see, they replaced them. So, and we used them up to this year. The sixth. We just had our dance. And then he played for us. He really did. The band is very good. Very good.
It looked like better than ever. And I'm really proud because he was so proud of his band and to let it go down, it would be a shame. But they're really keeping it up.

Oh, they're keeping it up. Very good. I often ask him what he would do in his band when he'd be gone. He says, well, I tried to teach the youngsters, but they won't listen. I say, but please leave somebody in your place. Just don't pass on and don't, you know, don't leave that to someone. So, but Eddie French. Albert French. Albert French. He really, and the one who sings on the mic. I don't know his name, but he sings all the Creole favorites.
All the Creole. All the. Brother Cornbread. His name is Joseph Thomas, but they call him.

Thomas. That's right. Albert Thomas. Yeah, yeah. George Thomas. George Thomas. George Thomas. He's the one that sings all the Creole songs. Yeah. He's old. And so they have a beautiful, wonderful band. Oh. And they played all the old pieces. This is funny.

You know, recently they said about the old musicians, they didn't have very many left. But you would be surprised how many they do have left that no one. I know quite a few right around here. Oh yeah. And I bet there's a lot still that you don't know that has valuable information. Oh yeah. Oh yeah. That's right. They're living. They're very old, but they're here. What kind of music do you prefer? Well, I do love jazz music. Well, it's everything in its place, but I do love Dixieland jazz in preference to progressive, or even rock and roll. I do love it. I'm not saying that because you were interviewing us, but it's a thing I always liked from a child. And of course, my aunt, living with us all these years, she played only that type of music. So naturally, I guess it just stayed imprinted in us. And it's what I really love. And you, Mrs. Senegal? I prefer jazz music. I hope it never dies out. Yeah. They sing. I prefer Stixieland music. I see some youngsters never working on a lot.
Because if you're not even dancing, it peps to you.

You know, the youngsters claim that they are going head over here for rock and roll. But some of our members bring their children and their grandchildren and give them invitations to our ball. And I noticed they enjoy themselves mighty well with that Dixieland music. Oh, more than their own dances. And they come every year. Yes, indeed. So they enjoy it, but I guess because rock and roll has taken over so much, they think they like it best. But actually, I think deep down in them, they like them for Dixieland. Yes. It's just in them. They will come around where a band's playing, or you'll see them in the second line. There'll be kids following a parade band or something, and they're certainly enjoying it, whether they'll admit it or not. Which proves that Dixieland is best. I mean, if they didn't enjoy it, they wouldn't bother to come around.

Well, there was a white group who followed Papa Celeste everywhere he went. He'd go to Baton Rouge. There would be a bus load there with them. I don't know where they were from. They were from Tulane or where. Don't you remember when he went out there for the concert? Oh, about 15 or 20, even more, following him, wherever he'd go. He'd go and really have him to go out there at this concert he was giving. And we saw that whole bus load of young white girls and boys. And they told me they followed him everywhere he went. They just liked his music.
You know, we haven't hardly talked to you at all. The ladies are keeping you quiet over there.
You ought to say something. You ought to say something. What kind of music do you prefer yourself?

Well, really, I love jazz music, Dixon Land music, I like dance music. Of course, that's what I've been following all my days. I always did dance with Bob Bill and Dixon Land music and jazz music. And jazz at that time was hard to go so.
Where were you born?
Well, I was born right early.
Did we get your birthday? I don't think we did.
Well, let me see. I think we have.
We got her, is it? Yeah.
I think we have.
You mind asking again?
Yeah, I don't mind you asking because I'm very young yet. Okay. 73. You're 73. 73. Born 1889, February 2nd, so I'm 73 now.
And what bands did you hear in New Iberia as you were growing up?

Well, in New Iberia at that time we had a band composed of the accordion. Oh, yeah. Mostly accordion music. That's the band there, accordion music and the guitar. Guitar and accordion. Yes. And finally we went on up to the halls, you know. Started to go in the halls. And Buck Johnson came in the band. He organized the band. Called Buck Johnson's band. So he started. And then he came in with the halls and the sliding tramboles and the brass band. That was after accordion and the guitar. And we had balls after balls. Every Saturday night was a big ball. Every Saturday night. That was a ball night. So we enjoyed that. That's why the quadrille really was ball out there. That was a quadrille every Saturday night.
What about those accordion players and guitar players? Do you remember any of their names?
Yeah, I know one player's name. A fellow used to be a professional at an accordion. His name was Lily.

Lily. His name was Lily. Do you remember bands from neighboring cities like, say, E. Van Thomas from Outta Crowley? Did you ever hear him? No, I don't remember. I just wondered if you'd ever heard of him. Mostly Bunk you remember.
Yeah, because after I got 17 years old I left him.
Oh, I see.
Then I came out of school.
Bunk was out there before you were 17? Oh, yeah. He must have gone mighty early. He must have been a young man himself.
No, no, he was. About 15 or 16 he was playing music. Yeah, sure, yeah.
Well, that's funny. He really got around. He was a lot of places.
Oh, yes. He went to St. Louis with his band. He went to Chicago with his band. He went all of them. He went here with his band. He used to go all around with his band. He didn't use it.
New York? I know you made a big hit in New York in 1945.
Oh, he was professional when he got to New York. He was professional. He was a big-timer. He really was a professional. He used to play. I think Satchimo used to play with him, too.
The other musicians say that. Yeah. That he learned from Bunk.

Bunk Jones. Bunk Jones was the father of those guys. He comes to music. So many of them, I can't recall right now exactly that band. He played music with Bunk Jones. He was a fine player. A good mixer. He was very charming, too. He was a fellow who gave his heart out to everybody else and leave himself in the morning. He really did that. He used to give away all he made. Way around the last. On the last part, he found out he was getting old. He came to me. He said, you know, Calvary. I said, I don't know. I've done a lot of good work. I've done plenty of money, but I don't have any money. I've done enough. I don't even want a home. I said, well, you don't have any. At that time, my folks were dead. I said, I'd like to sell you by. He was getting prepared to buy the home at that time. He said, you know, I got $4,000. I had to buy it. I said, you know, we sell it to you for four thousand. He went off. Well, my brother, he wouldn't agree to run on the home at that time. He drifted off. He finally died before he got the home. Yeah. Because he lived just about a block from us. He was raised up from us. Just about a block from us. They were all raised up together. We all went to school together. He went to school with us. We went on and on and on. He spent all his time in music. All his time in Spanish music. He looked at half and half days. He left to build for dear

pages.label: 003_Mr. and Mrs. A.C. Synigal and B. Bozant Interview, 1962-05-17 Part 3

blocks.x: The Second World The Second World The Second World This is the third reel. We're interviewing the Senegals here, and Mrs. Ozan.
Bozan. Bozan. Which one?
Ozan. And it's May the 17th, 1962.

segments.title: Opening of second reel and the Synigal home as Fiesta headquarters
segments.summary: Recording is set up on 17 May 1962 at the Synigal home; the women are introduced and Mrs. Synigal describes the house as fiesta headquarters with a patio meeting room.

segments.title: Mrs. Synigal's birth in the family home on Coord Street
segments.summary: She was born in New Orleans in the house where her father and grandmother's other grandchildren were also born, a family custom.

segments.title: First Creole Fiesta parade and the first Mademoiselle Fiesta
segments.summary: The fiesta had a parade from its first year, with rented fruit wagons, young girls as Mademoiselle Fiesta, and floats and carriages added as it grew.

segments.title: Soirees dansantes and the rice-cake 'calas' at the block festival
segments.summary: Mrs. Synigal explains the soirees and the first outside affair, a block festival where two ladies cooked calas, which sold out.

segments.title: Trying to find the cala recipe
segments.summary: The interviewer offers to look for a recipe and mentions the book Gumbo Ya Ya.

segments.title: From block festivals to soiree dansants in club halls
segments.summary: Square dancing by the Holy Family Sisters, rain ending the street festivals, and the move of the soiree to club halls.

segments.title: The September fiesta tea with Professor Blanchett and local performers
segments.summary: The fiesta opens with a September tea; last year pianist Oceola Blanchett, a dancer and singers performed, making it almost a concert.

segments.chapter: Papa Celestin and the fiesta bands
segments.title: Getting Congo Square and the first concert with Papa Celestin and Lizzie Miles
segments.summary: Mrs. Synigal tells how she won use of Congo Square from the city, and how Celestin's band and Lizzie Miles reconciled at the first concert.

segments.chapter: Papa Celestin and the fiesta bands
segments.title: Later concert at Claiborne and Columbus with Celestin's band
segments.summary: They recall a third-year concert on Claiborne and Columbus and Celestin's band playing.

segments.chapter: Papa Celestin and the fiesta bands
segments.title: Albert French's band and singer Joseph 'Cornbread' Thomas
segments.summary: The fiesta has used a band every year, now Albert French's, with Thomas singing Creole songs.

segments.title: Preference for Dixieland over rock and roll
segments.summary: The women say they love Dixieland jazz and that young people enjoy it despite rock and roll.

segments.title: White followers of Papa Celestin's band
segments.summary: A busload of young white fans followed Celestin everywhere, including Baton Rouge.

segments.title: A.C. Synigal's taste in jazz and dance music
segments.summary: Asked his preference, Mr. Synigal says he loves jazz and Dixieland dance music.

segments.title: A.C. Synigal's birth date
segments.summary: He was born 2 February 1889 and is 73.

segments.title: Bands in New Iberia: accordion, guitar and early brass bands
segments.summary: He recalls accordion and guitar music, Bunk Johnson organizing a band, Saturday-night balls and quadrilles, and an accordionist named Lily.

segments.title: Bunk Johnson's early career and travels
segments.summary: Bunk was playing at 15 or 16, later toured widely and was a professional in New York; Armstrong is said to have played with him.

segments.title: Bunk Johnson's generosity and the home he never bought
segments.summary: Synigal remembers Bunk as a fine, charming player who gave away his money and died before buying a home; the block ends in garbled ASR looping.

segments.title: Start of third reel
segments.summary: The third reel begins with the Synigals and Mrs. Bozan present, dated 17 May 1962.
